articles.title: Newly obtained footage shows Iran attack on major U.S. post in Kuwait
articles.summary: CBS News obtained new video from a person on the ground showing an Iranian attack on a U.S. base at the beginning of the war.
articles.body:
Washington — New videos obtained exclusively by CBS News show Iranian attacks on a major U.S. military base in Kuwait as the war with Iran kicked off seven months ago. American forces faced ballistic missiles, drones and what witnesses described as Iranian F-5 fighter jets.

The footage obtained by CBS News was recorded by a person stationed on the ground at Camp Buehring, and captures the moments of impact and their explosive aftermath. Damage to buildings and military equipment can also be seen in the videos.

The attacks on Camp Buehring offer a window into the strain Iranian attacks placed on American forces during the opening days of the war. CBS News has learned that soldiers defending the base ran critically low on .50-caliber ammunition as some soldiers were repositioned into the Udari Desert in Kuwait. Two soldiers were injured by lightning there in late April, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.

Contacted by CBS News, U.S. Central Command, the primary unit which oversees American military operations across the Middle East, declined to comment.

The Pentagon did not comment, but pointed back to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's comments on March 4 regarding the removal of U.S. troops from bases and the employment of defensive measures.

"As we built up offensive combat power, we moved the vast majority of American troops — over 90% of Americans that were on our bases — what we say off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire," Hegseth told reporters in March.

Camp Buehring, or CBKU, sits about 25 miles from the Iraqi border and has for more than two decades served as a major staging ground for American forces deploying across the Middle East.

CBS News authenticated the videos using metadata embedded in the files and compared the footage to other photographs showing damage to the base.

Ahead of the war, sources said most of the roughly 7,000 troops there were moved elsewhere — as were the majority of U.S. forces in Kuwait — as a part of the Pentagon's "get off the X" plan, military shorthand for moving away from a position vulnerable to attack.

Once the war started, Iranian attacks, some originating from Iraq, repeatedly threatened the installation. Missiles and drones forced soldiers into bunkers. Three U.S. service members told CBS News that Iranian F-5 fighter jets were also used during the attacks, a detail first reported in April by NBC News.

"They ran so close to us I could see their helmets," the eyewitness described. "They came in, they hit us, and then took off."

While most of the U.S. service members were moved off of Camp Buehring, a tranche of more than 100 soldiers stayed behind. The service members feared the isolated base was ill-equipped to handle a mass-casualty event if the attacks continued.

"They hit us bad," the source told CBS News on condition of anonymity because of the military's strict media restrictions. "It was horrible. There were a lot of brave guys who stayed to fight there — and people at home don't know what happened. We had to abandon the base."

A senior Army official working in logistics, managing operations from another post in Kuwait, confirmed to CBS News there were concerns about the availability of .50 caliber ammunition and other "exquisite" munitions like Patriot missile batteries.

The decision ultimately was to leave. Service members packed up, loading their vehicles with whatever equipment they could and drove at night deep into the Kuwaiti desert. Their remote locations would emerge as forward operating bases, or "FOBs," where the soldiers would remain indefinitely.

No one was killed by enemy fire at Camp Buehring or at the FOBs, but several were injured, including two soldiers who were struck by lightning in desert sandstorms. One soldier suffered burns after the direct strike while the other suffered a ruptured eardrum, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.

Before the lightning strike, Army leaders had been trying to move the troops out of the area, but were not able to do so quickly enough. In May, the soldiers left the FOBs for Camp Arifjan, and then relocated to other positions both in and out of the Middle East.

"CBKU got demolished," the source added. "They need to do an investigation. How come no one came to reinforce us?"

The Defense Department's inspector general last month released a report on the war with Iran that revealed "equipment losses" worth up to $3.7 billion — including nearly 60 aircraft. On Monday, the Congressional Research Service, which provides nonpartisan analysis to members of Congress, reported that 81 fixed or rotary-wing aircraft including drone assets had been lost or damaged by Iran since February, according to news reports and statements from the Defense Department.

In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to Congress, the inspector general added that U.S. Central Command had reported Iranian strikes at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.

Although strikes were mentioned in the report, pictures and videos of any impact zones have been extremely limited. Beyond Camp Buehring, CBS News earlier obtained exclusive photos of damage at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.

CBS News has also reported extensively on the deadliest attack of the war against U.S. troops at the Port of Shuaiba, which killed six American service members.

articles.title: In Canada, a 16-year-old needed to be air-rescued after following AI-planned hiking route onto 'Widowmaker'
articles.summary: By chance, North Shore Rescue volunteers were on Crown Mountain doing helicopter training.
articles.body:
A 16-year-old hiking alone in British Columbia showed the limits of AI trip planning. After using artificial intelligence to map a route up Crown Mountain, he got trapped on a cliff along a climbing route called the "Widowmaker" before rescue crews lifted him out.

According to North Shore News , rescuers got a call just before 3:30 p.m. about a teen stranded on Crown Mountain, roughly a 40-minute drive north of Vancouver.

Search manager Paul Markey said the hiker started from Grouse Mountain at about 8 a.m. and planned to reach Crown Mountain through a gully but instead wound up in steep climbing terrain below a cliff.

"It turns out that this hiker had somehow got far off the Crown hiking route (we are unclear exactly how/where) and became stranded on a climbing route known as the 'Widowmaker,' at the base of its final headwall," North Shore Rescue wrote in a Facebook post .

The post continued: "The two rescue techs were inserted above the subjects' location, as the subject was too close to the vertical wall (i.e., lacking the necessary helicopter rotor clearance to deliver the techs to his exact location). When on the ground, the crew established an anchor and one member was belayed to the subject. There, the member established additional protection and was able to move the subject to a suitable extraction point."

He was then hoisted off the mountain, and the mission ended shortly before 6:30 p.m.

"The boy was very scared. He definitely feared for his life," Markey told North Shore News.

In a similar instance on California's Mount Shasta, three hikers had to be rescued after relying on Google's Gemini to plan their trip, ABC News reported. "They were advised by Gemini to bring far less food and water than their group required, especially when their planned eight-hour ascent became a multiday ordeal," the Siskiyou County Sheriff's Office said.

Recently, Meta and OpenAI introduced new AI agents, pitching them as tools for tasks such as travel booking and shopping.

Markey said hikers should use familiar route-planning apps such as Gaia GPS, CalTopo, or AllTrails instead of AI directions. North Shore News did not identify which AI tool the teen used.

By chance, North Shore Rescue volunteers were on Crown Mountain doing helicopter training.

"Be cautious when getting routes and information suggested through AI," Markey told North Shore News. "You can't just blindly follow what AI is proposing to you. You need to question the information and just see whether it makes sense or not."

AI use can go badly wrong in nature and other high-stakes settings, though it can be useful as well.

• Veteran forager Alan Bergo warned that AI can cause life-threatening effects in the wild.

• Google users said a dangerous response on lug-nut torque showed how bad AI advice can be.

• At Cambridge University, engineers built a crucial landslide-detection tool for disasters.

• Scientists are using AI to predict weather patterns such as El Niño earlier.

• Google's FireSat looks to detect wildfires rapidly so first responders can move faster.

articles.title: Holborn and St Pancras by-election under way as polls open
articles.summary: Voters in north London are going to the polls to choose a new MP after Sir Keir Starmer resigned.
articles.body:
Voting is under way in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election as candidates from across the political spectrum vie to become its new MP.

About 30 polling stations - at churches and community centres - in the north London constituency opened at 07:00 BST and will close at 22:00, when a count will begin.

The seat became vacant after former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down to focus on a role in international affairs .

Some 15 candidates are standing in the by-election, one of whom is an independent.

Voters will need to show a form of acceptable ID - such as a driving licence or passport - to be able to vote.

articles.summary: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize, while acknowledging that he remains unsure whether the Norwegian Nobel
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize, while acknowledging that he remains unsure whether the Norwegian Nobel Committee will select him for the 2026 award.Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump said the announcement was imminent and suggested that the committee may not favour him.“I don't know what their decision is going to be,” Trump said of the 2026 award, which the Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce on Friday. “They have a ​reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me,” he added.“It is about that time,” Trump remarked. “But I was very honoured to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump.”This is not the first time Trump has said he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize. Trump has repeatedly claimed that his diplomatic interventions since returning to the White House have helped resolve multiple international conflicts.“I’ve done stuff that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging, I’m just telling you the facts. No president has probably ever settled any wars. I settled eight wars.”“But, whether I get it or not, I have done far more. And I think it would be a great discredit to them. And I’m not saying that out of scorn, I’m saying that when you settle eight wars, and nobody’s never,” he added.Trump has also credited his administration’s trade and economic pressure, including threatened tariffs, with pushing countries towards diplomatic engagement. However, his claims about the extent of those diplomatic achievements have faced challenges, with conflicts continuing or resurfacing in several regions.Trump also criticised former US President Barack Obama, who received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2009. “Obama got it, and he didn’t do anything,” Trump stated. “He still doesn’t know what he got it for. He got it when he got elected, right at the beginning, and he had no idea why he got it.”Trump also referred to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who won last year’s Nobel Peace Prize.“Last time they gave it to a young lady who’s a fabulous person, and she said she didn’t deserve it, that I deserved it, and she gave it to me,” Trump said.Machado has previously praised Trump and said she wanted to share the honour with him. However, the Norwegian Nobel Institute has clarified that the Nobel Peace Prize itself cannot be transferred or shared.“A Nobel Prize cannot be revoked nor transferred to others. Once the laureate or laureates are announced, the decision is final,” said Erik Aasheim, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Nobel Institute.Aasheim added that while the prize itself cannot be transferred, laureates are free to dispose of the prize money as they wish.The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner will be announced on October 9, with the award ceremony scheduled for December 10. The prize is decided independently by the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: The legendary Shakespeare Ranch in Nevada, first listed for $188 million in 2024 is now asking $125 million; the 700-acre property has a 465-foot private pier, multiple homes and a barn built in 1873
articles.summary: One of Lake Tahoe's most expensive properties is back in focus after a major reduction in its asking price.
articles.body: One of Lake Tahoe's most expensive properties is back in focus after a major reduction in its asking price. Shakespeare Ranch, a historic 700-acre estate on the Nevada side of the lake, was listed for $188 million in 2024, SF Gate reported. Two years later, the property is being offered for $125 million, a reduction of $63 million, as its owners continue to look for a buyer.Located in Glenbrook, an exclusive community on Lake Tahoe's eastern shore, the ranch includes several lakefront homes, guest cottages, horse corrals and a private pier extending 465 feet into a sheltered bay. It also has a barn built in 1873, which remains one of the property's most distinctive features.According to the report, the ranch has attracted celebrities and even US presidents over the years, particularly through its annual rodeo. Former President George Bush reportedly visited the property and remarked, "They don't make barns like this in Texas."Despite its history, location and facilities, the estate has yet to find a buyer. This is particularly notable because luxury homes along Lake Tahoe's Nevada shoreline have been selling quickly in recent years. Even after the price reduction, Shakespeare Ranch remains the most expensive property listed in the Lake Tahoe area.What makes Shakespeare Ranch different?Shakespeare Ranch combines a large waterfront estate with buildings and facilities that reflect its long history. Unlike a conventional luxury home, the property includes multiple residences spread across the ranch, with several overlooking Lake Tahoe.Surrounding a courtyard is a collection of cottages and guest houses. Horses also graze in corrals near a meadow. The estate also has direct access to the lake through its 465-foot private pier.The barn dating back to 1873 is central to the property's identity. It has been associated with the ranch's annual rodeo, an event that has drawn visitors from across US.The estate's setting in Glenbrook also adds to its appeal. The community is a private enclave for wealthy residents, comparable to Incline Village, another well-known luxury residential area on the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe.The struggle to find a buyerThe ranch first entered the market in October 2024 with an asking price of $188 million. At the time, it was the most expensive listing in Lake Tahoe, coinciding with growing interest in the region among the wealthy.Since then, the luxury housing market along Nevada's Lake Tahoe shoreline has remained active. According to the report, multimillion-dollar waterfront properties have been selling rapidly, particularly over the past two or three years.Much of this demand has been linked to the real estate boom in San Francisco, driven partly by wealth generated in the artificial intelligence industry. Some wealthy buyers from California have also been looking towards Nevada because of its more favourable tax environment.The reduced figure still places the ranch well above other expensive properties currently being marketed around the lake.Taxes and Lake Tahoe's property marketTax considerations have become an important factor for wealthy Californians purchasing homes across the state border in Nevada.California is preparing to vote on a proposed wealth tax, while Nevada's comparatively lenient tax laws have made it attractive to buyers considering their long-term financial arrangements."Taxes are a huge part of it," Christine Perry, a real estate agent with Christie's International who works with wealthy clients in Silicon Valley and Lake Tahoe, told SFGATE.Perry said one of her clients had purchased a home on the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe but spent very little time there. Although the client was not ready to leave the Bay Area, the purchase was intended as an investment in the future and potentially an alternative place to live. "I think a lot of people are trying to prepare themselves for the future," Perry said.This interest has also encouraged families who have owned waterfront properties for generations to consider selling their estates.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Most UK diplomats to leave East Jerusalem consulate, Israel says, as Miliband says 'vital services' to remain
articles.summary: Israel said in September it would act in response to UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
articles.body:
Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission".

"We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the consul general would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity".

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been "temporarily withdrawn" for security reasons, but stressed the mission will "work with the Palestinian people".

Israel said in September it would shut the consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.

The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement.

The consulate, which was first established in 1838, handles UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.

It is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the country had implemented measures announced on 8 September in response to UK sanctions.

"The British Consulate in Jerusalem is closing its operations today. Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed," he wrote on social media.

However, the British flag could still be seen outside on Thursday morning, and several staff were seen entering.

Saar said talks with the UK government had resulted in agreement on certain principles, including that "the consul general and 20 diplomats (including the consul general) are ending their duties and will leave Israel."

But Saar acknowledged that the building is "the property of the British government" and said Israel had authorised "a task force of only seven diplomats with a very limited scope of activity" to operate in the building.

As a result of this agreement with the UK, he said, "no steps will be taken against Israel".

Israeli media had been reporting that the UK had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats from London - raising the prospect of further damaging bilateral relations.

This agreement is a compromise of sorts and means - for the moment - the heat has been taken out of a dispute that could have further worsened UK-Israel relations.

Israel can claim that the British Consulate is "closing its operations". A score of British diplomats, including the consul general, are leaving.

But Miliband says they are going only temporarily and only for their safety and security. He continues to insist Israel has no legal right to close the consulate.

"The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory," Miliband wrote in a statement.

Following discussions with the Israeli government, he said, the building "will not be closing" and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from Thursday.

However Miliband said an understanding had not been reached on "necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises".

"Accordingly the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security," he added.

The Foreign Office said the seven UK diplomats who remain will be "independent and operational" and continue to deliver vital services. Israel said they will provide "only a limited scope of activity".

FCDO sources described the deal as a "good outcome" because the entire operation was not closing, as had been threatened. They said that maintaining a UK presence would help build back the mission in the future.

Speaking to the Today programme, Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty explained: "The building remains open. We retain our presence, we continue having staff able to do important work engaging with the Palestinian Authority... and we are engaging in ongoing conversations with Israel on this matter."

Asked if this was a political fudge, Doughty said "you can see what's changed in terms of a name but crucially our presence remains", adding that the "policies towards this Israeli government, which we fundamentally disagree with" would continue.

The foreign secretary made clear the UK reserved the right to take what he called "reciprocal action" but said he would not do so while "discussions are under way and credible". That means any UK retaliation is unlikely before Israel's elections later this month.

articles.title: Three rare snake species bred at Prague Zoo for the first time; two groups of young descend from animals seized from smugglers
articles.summary: In late July 2026, Prague Zoo announced a rare triple success in its reptile collection, three snake species that had never bred there before produced
articles.body: In late July 2026, Prague Zoo announced a rare triple success in its reptile collection, three snake species that had never bred there before produced young. Rough-scaled pythons hatched from a clutch of eggs, Nosy Komba ground boas gave birth to live young, and Tartar sand boas added a litter of their own. The animals come from three very different corners of the world, from the gorges of north-western Australia to the island of Madagascar and the sand dunes of Asia. Here is what happened, why the story matters for conservation and wildlife protection.How three snake species hatched or were born for the first time at Prague Zoo in the Troja districtPrague Zoo announced on 27 July 2026 that three snake species had reproduced there for the first time in its history. According to the zoo, a clutch of rough-scaled python eggs produced two young. A female Nosy Komba ground boa gave birth to ten, while a female Tartar sand boa delivered four. The Madagascan species appeared under different names in the press; the Prague Daily News called it the Madagascar boa and the brown boa, whereas the zoo's own name, used here, is the Nosy Komba ground boa.Rough-scaled pythons from north-western AustraliaThe zoo's announcement describes the rough-scaled python as a small, tree-dwelling snake. Scientists discovered it in 1981, and until 2007 it was known from only ten individuals, the zoo explained.It is a relict species, a survivor of a habitat that once reached further. It lives in humid forests and has persisted only in the deep gorges of the Kimberley region in north-western Australia. The zoo stresses that its range is among the smallest of any snake in the world. For a species this scarce and this little studied, two healthy hatchlings carry real weight.Nosy Komba ground boas from Madagascar give birth to ten youngsThe official announcement identifies the Nosy Komba ground boa as endemic to the island of Madagascar, and says the young are more colourful and striking than the adults.The species also has a revealing scientific history. Prague Zoo notes that it was once classed as a subspecies of the Madagascar tree boa, until genetic testing showed the two have been evolving separately for millions of years. A litter of ten therefore represents a full, distinct species rather than a regional variety.Tartar sand boas, the sand-swimming burrowers of Asian desertsThe third species spends its life underground. According to the zoo, the Tartar sand boa comes from the semi-deserts and deserts of the Middle East and Central Asia, and is known as a "sand swimmer". Its reduced eyes and cylindrical body are adaptations to moving through loose sand. The announcement said the female's four offspring delighted her keepers.They descend from snakes confiscated from wildlife smugglersThe story has a sombre background. Petr Velenský, the zoo's Curator of Reptiles, told the announcement that all three rearings were welcome, but the pythons and the sand boas meant a little more to him. Both sets of young are the grandchildren of snakes confiscated from smugglers, the pythons in Vienna and the sand boas in Cologne.Velenský described the successful breeding of these descendants as "a nice continuation of what is otherwise quite a sad story". It shows how animals seized from illegal wildlife trafficking can support carefully managed breeding in zoos.Where visitors could find the snakes at Prague ZooWhen the news was released, the zoo pointed visitors to three locations. The rough-scaled python lived in the Darwin Crater exhibit. Opposite it, in the Terrarium building, visitors could see the Nosy Komba ground boa. The Tartar sand boa was in the upper part of the zoo, in a small pavilion within the Gobi exhibit.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A 2,600-acre South Carolina timber property at the rivers where Revolutionary War commander Francis Marion hid from British forces has been transferred to the state, advancing a 7,600-acre conservation project with 60+ miles of riverfront
articles.summary: A 2,600-acre timber property in South Carolina, located near the rivers where Revolutionary War commander Francis Marion once hid from British forces, has
articles.body: A 2,600-acre timber property in South Carolina, located near the rivers where Revolutionary War commander Francis Marion once hid from British forces, has been transferred to the state's Department of Natural Resources. The land, known as River Forks, forms part of a larger 7,600-acre conservation project that aims to protect wildlife habitats, historic sites and areas that help reduce flooding.The Open Space Institute (OSI), a non-profit conservation organisation, transferred the property to the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources (SCDNR). According to Vise Voter, the transfer, announced on Tuesday includes 11 miles of riverfront and marks the first phase of the Snow's Island Assemblage conservation project.The wider project covers two properties in Florence County including the 5,000-acre Snow's Island and the adjoining 2,600-acre River Forks timber tract. Together, they include more than 60 miles of riverfront along the Lynches and Great Pee Dee Rivers. OSI acquired both properties in 2024.Francis Marion and the swampsSnow's Island is located where the Lynches and Great Pee Dee Rivers meet. During the American Revolutionary War, Marion and his militia used the area's remote swamps as a base for military operations against British troops.The surrounding waterways and wetlands provided a place from which Marion could organise raids. According to OSI, his militia launched several attacks from the area, including a major assault on the British garrison at Georgetown, located downstream along the Pee Dee River.The conservation project is intended to protect this historic landscape while eventually allowing people to visit the area. Once the land becomes part of the state's Heritage Preserve and Wildlife Management Area programmes, visitors will have opportunities to explore the swamps associated with Marion's wartime activities.The property, however, remains closed to the public while SCDNR works towards completing the larger conservation project.7,600-acre wildlife habitatThe Snow's Island Assemblage contains several types of natural habitats, including bottomland hardwood forests, upland pine forests and floodplains. These areas support wildlife and connect with other protected lands in the region.The 2,600-acre River Forks property alone provides habitat for 140 high-priority conservation species, including 15 species listed as at risk under federal or state classifications.Among the wildlife associated with the wider conservation area are the Swallow-tailed Kite and Spotted Turtle. Protecting such a large stretch of connected land is intended to help animals move between habitats without the barriers created when natural areas are divided into smaller parcels.The project also strengthens an existing network of protected land that includes the 25,000-acre Woodbury Wildlife Management Area.Flood protection from forestFlood protection is another major reason behind the conservation effort. The property contains extensive forested wetlands and floodplains that can hold large quantities of water during heavy rainfall.These floodplains work like natural sponges, absorbing water when rivers rise and releasing it gradually. This helps reduce the amount of floodwater moving downstream at once.The importance of these natural floodplains became clear during Hurricane Florence in 2018, when severe flooding affected parts of South Carolina.Flood data published in the Journal of South Carolina Water Resources showed that the large floodplain between the Pee Dee, Lynches and Little Pee Dee Rivers stored more than one million acre-feet of water during the hurricane. That water was released gradually over ten days, helping protect communities downstream.The Snow's Island Assemblage lies within this floodplain, making its protection important for the region's long-term flood management.Funding the conservationThe project involves cooperation between conservation organisations, state agencies, local authorities and private foundations.Funding for the River Forks acquisition included $3 million from the US Fish and Wildlife Service. The wider conservation effort also received support from the South Carolina Office of Resilience, South Carolina Conservation Bank, Darla Moore Foundation and Knobloch Family Foundation.Florence County Council voted in July 2024 to contribute $1.5 million from its capital sales tax fund towards acquiring the Snow's Island Assemblage. According to OSI, this was the county's first investment in land conservation.The properties were previously owned by Manulife Investment Management and Weyerhaeuser before OSI acquired them in 2024.The transfer of River Forks is the first stage of bringing the entire Snow's Island Assemblage under state management. The remaining land is expected to be transferred to SCDNR in early 2027. Once the process is completed, the state plans to manage the protected landscape through its Wildlife Management Area and Heritage Trust programmes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Police to issue interview letters as part of Garvaghy Road investigation
articles.summary: Police have said they are moving to the next phase of the investigation in connection with the Drumcree dispute.
articles.body:
Police have said they will begin issuing letters regarding an interview process to people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the unlawful protests blocking the Garvaghy Road in Portadown.

A statement issued on Thursday said police were moving to the next phase of their investigation in connection with the Drumcree dispute.

Unionist politicians have called for the police to take action against First Minister Michelle O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin politicians who took part in the protest against the Orange Order march.

A Sinn Féin spokesperson said they were aware of the statement and would not be making any further comment due to the ongoing investigation.

O'Neill has previously defended joining the protests, saying she was "proud to stand with the residents" and "when the law is wrong, I will stand firmly against it".

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) statement does not name anyone it plans to issue a letter to.

Assistant Chief Constable Davy Beck said police had been "methodically working" through the evidence collected so far in its investigation.

He added: "This work will now proceed to the next phase where individuals will receive letters regarding the interview process. I am satisfied that this step does not have an impact on the ongoing Judicial Review, which I respect.

"As this is a live criminal investigation we will not be making any further comment at this time."

Earlier, politicians cautioned against escalating the parading dispute, following a warning from residents that it could lead to issues with other marches.

It's the twelfth day of deadlock between residents of the Garvaghy Road and the local district lodge of the Orange Order over the proposed march.

On Wednesday, the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition (GRRC) said the disagreement was "no longer just about the Garvaghy Road" after meeting 11 other nationalist residents' groups.

Several politicians have said they do not want the dispute to spark other disagreements about parades in other locations.

Claire Hanna, the leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme there was a need to "get a grip" of the situation "before it engulfs the wider political system".

She called on the Secretary of State, Sir Chris Bryant, to withdraw permission for the parade but said that "sensible voices within unionism" should "ask the lodge to reconsider, because there is the potential for this to scale out into other areas".

Jon Burrows, the leader of the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) said he thought it would be a "mistake" for the secretary of state to get involved, but said politicians should make a "collective appeal to contain" the dispute in Drumcree.

"What we need to hear is political leaders saying we must not open these disputes across the country."

The Northern Ireland Office (NIO) has said the secretary of state is continuing to engage with all parties for a resolution.

Sinn Féin MP Chris Hazzard said there had been warnings that "opening up Drumcree" could "unravel agreements everywhere else".

"Accommodating sensitive parades relies entirely on mutual respect. We have to see an injection here of mutual respect," he added.

Jonathan Buckley, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) MLA for Upper Bann, said he wanted to see "mediated outcomes where residents can live and accommodate one another".

"I want to de-escalate. I want to see accommodation, and I want to see this issue resolved."

In Londonderry, dialogue around parading has come to be seen as crucial, and has resulted in an accommodation between residents, businesses and the Apprentice Boys.

That accommodation, developed in the late 1990s and early 2000s, has become known as the Derry Model.

It relies on direct engagement rather than a reliance on Parades Commission rulings.

East Londonderry DUP MP Gregory Campbell told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme he did not believe that model was in jeopardy.

"No, I don't think it will be – there seems to be an attempt to completely change the narrative here," he said.

But Foyle Sinn Féin MLA Ciara Ferguson said there is " genuine nervousness" in Derry.

"I would be slightly fearful that it has got the potential to unravel," she said.

The Apprentice Boys' hold two parades in Derry city centre - in August and in December – each year, marking the beginning and end of the 1689 Siege of the city.

It is more than a week since the decision to allow an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road on Sunday, 27 September.

That morning, up to 1,000 people - including politicians such as Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west.

Since then, residents have maintained a constant presence around the road while Orangemen have also repeatedly tried to march the route before being turned back by police.

The stand-off has caused considerable political fallout in Northern Ireland, with First Minister O'Neill facing a vote of no confidence over her involvement in the protest.

The vote is due to fail due to it requiring cross-community support at the Northern Ireland Assembly.

Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.

Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order for the past three decades.

Earlier this year the Parades Commission decided that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place after its original decision to stop the march was overturned in court.

Meanwhile, the Court of Appeal is considering its ruling in a legal challenge brought by the residents to block the march going ahead.

articles.summary: KALYAN: The appointment of Shailesh Kulkarni as city engineer of the Kalyan-Dombivli Municipal Corporation (KDMC) has raised questions in civic circles
articles.body: KALYAN: The appointment of Shailesh Kulkarni as city engineer of the Kalyan-Dombivli Municipal Corporation (KDMC) has raised questions in civic circles over the seniority criteria followed for the key post.Kulkarni has been given additional charge of the post, which fell vacant after Anita Pardeshi was transferred to the Gram Sadak Yojana in Nashik. Executive Engineer of Town Planning Surendra Tengale, ranked fourth in the seniority list, was also in contention. Kulkarni is seventh, with six officers ahead of him.The civil engineering department has 12 sanctioned posts for executive engineers. Besides Tengale, the seniority list includes Sandeep Tambe, Shashim Kedar, Shailesh Malekar and Prasad Sakhdev. Tengale and Kulkarni are from the open category. Tengale has handled town planning and Smart City projects and has around three years of service left.The decision has prompted allegations that the seniority list was overlooked and other eligible officers were bypassed.KDMC commissioner Abhinav Goel, however, told TOI, "The city engineer's post is meant to be filled by an officer appointed by the state government. Until the state government issues an order appointing an officer as city engineer, Kulkarni has been given additional charge," he said.Goel said some officers senior to Kulkarni are nearing retirement, while others are already holding similar posts."There is no mandatory rule that the senior-most officer has to be given the post of city engineer. Appointments can also be made based on an officer's capabilities and suitability," he said.The issue has also brought attention to a precedent in Navi Mumbai, where a city engineer from the electrical department has reportedly held the post. If the same criteria are applied at KDMC, civic circles have questioned whether Prashant Bhagwat, currently posted as additional city engineer in the Electricity department and senior to several officers in the hierarchy, could also be considered for the post.The city engineer plays a key role in preparing proposals for major civic infrastructure and development works before they are submitted to the commissioner for approval.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: On a 160-acre Nebraska farm parcel, one wind turbine and its equipment use about 1 acre; the developer says a typical 30-year lease averages $10,000 to $12,500 a year, versus about $600 for top-dollar corn on that acre
articles.summary: A farmer in Nebraska, United States, is earning additional income by leasing part of his agricultural land for a wind turbine.
articles.body: A farmer in Nebraska, United States, is earning additional income by leasing part of his agricultural land for a wind turbine. A wind energy company has leased his 160-acre property to install a wind turbine, but the turbine and its equipment take up only about one acre. The farmer can continue using the remaining 159 acres for agriculture.The financial difference is significant. According to the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA), the company behind the project says a typical 30-year lease pays an average of $10,000 to $12,500 a year. In comparison, even a highly productive acre of corn might bring in around $600 annually. The figures were shared in a case study published by NRECA in July 2021.The wind turbine is part of a project in Cuming County, Nebraska, where a local electricity provider wanted to produce some of its own power instead of buying all its electricity from larger suppliers. The company, Bluestem Energy Solutions, installed the turbine in 2019 and sells the electricity it produces to Cuming County Public Power District (CCPPD), which serves homes and businesses in the area.How does the farmer earn money?Matt Robinette, vice president of development at Bluestem Energy Solutions, explained that the company signs leases covering the entire piece of land, even though it needs only a small area for the turbine. "The landowner is free to utilize the other 159 acres for whatever purposes they prefer," Robinette said.The agreement lasts for 30 years, with an option to extend it. According to the company, a typical lease pays an average of $10,000 to $12,500 annually over this period. The payments start at a lower amount and gradually increase each year.Chet McWhorter, general manager of CCPPD, explained why the arrangement is financially attractive for the farmer. "Even if it was top dollar corn and the landowner was the best farmer in the world, he might be getting $600 an acre, so he's doing very well with the lease," McWhorter said.However, the $10,000 to $12,500 figure represents the company's typical lease payments, not the confirmed annual income of this particular farmer.Why wind turbine was installed on farmland?The idea began in 2016 when CCPPD was negotiating a new electricity supply agreement. The district wanted to produce some electricity locally to reduce its dependence on outside suppliers and keep costs more predictable.It first explored solar power and even installed solar panels on its office building to see how well they worked.However, the area frequently experiences cloudy and rainy weather, making a larger solar project less financially attractive. Adding batteries to store solar electricity would also have been too expensive at the time.The district then turned towards wind energy after one of its directors visited another wind turbine project in Nebraska.CCPPD initially considered owning a turbine itself, but the cost was too high. It eventually partnered with Bluestem Energy Solutions, which agreed to build, own and maintain the turbine.The project cost approximately $4.5 million, which Bluestem funded. CCPPD instead agreed to buy the electricity generated by the turbine for 30 years.2.5 megawatts of electricity producedThe wind turbine installed in Cuming County is a General Electric model capable of producing up to 2.5 megawatts of electricity.It stands on an 89-metre tower and reaches approximately 152 metres when one of its blades points straight upwards.According to the NRECA case study, the turbine was expected to generate around 10,950 megawatt-hours of electricity each year. CCPPD estimated that this would be enough to supply electricity to more than 900 homes.The turbine sends electricity to a nearby power station, from where it is supplied to local customers. This means the district does not need to purchase the same amount of electricity from its larger supplier.The turbine recorded a capacity factor of 56.17% in 2020. In simple terms, this measures how much electricity it actually generated compared with what it could have produced if it had operated at full capacity throughout the year.Benefits for the local communityThe benefits extend beyond the farmer receiving lease payments. According to the 2021 case study, the turbine had helped CCPPD reduce its annual electricity costs by around 3% to 4%.The district also estimated that the project would contribute more than $1 million to the local economy over its 30-year life.It brings in approximately $11,000 in additional property taxes each year, with 60% of that money going to public schools.The project also supports local businesses when maintenance workers visit the area and spend money on hotels, fuel and food.Bluestem is responsible for maintaining the turbine, so CCPPD does not have to pay separately for repairs or regular servicing.Another advantage is that the electricity price is agreed upon in advance. While the cost of electricity purchased from other suppliers can change, the wind power agreement gives the district a clearer idea of what it will pay in the coming years. "The nice thing about wind is we know exactly what it's going to cost," McWhorter said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: At least five arrested over Renoir museum theft
articles.summary: The two paintings by the French artist stolen in last month's heist have yet to be recovered.
articles.body:
At least five people have been arrested in France in connection with the theft of two paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir last month, local media report.

The two suspected burglars are said to be among them.

Two of the masterpieces stolen from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a suburb of Nice, have yet to be recovered. Two other works were abandoned by the thieves as they rushed to leave the museum.

The heist was the latest in a series of high-profile art thefts in Europe which thrust the security of galleries and museums into the spotlight.

The suspects cut through a fence to enter the museum's tree-lined grounds at dawn on 8 September, smashed a window to get inside, and used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings.

The two missing paintings are the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).

According to the Nice-Matin newspaper, which first broke the news of the arrests, the suspects could be part of an organised criminal gang. Some French news outlets, including Nice-Matin, say the number of those arrested is six.

Local prosecutors have declined to confirm the arrests when contacted by the BBC.

The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.

Opened in 1960, it was Renoir's last home before his death in 1919, and also features many things that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.

Several European museums and galleries have seen major thefts in recent months.

In August, paintings by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum in Italy, in a heist that lasted just three minutes. They were later recovered.

One of the most high-profile such incidents was in October last year, when France's crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris.

The thieves, disguised as construction workers, broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours. Using a angle-grinder to open display cases, they made off with €88m (£78m) of jewels that once belonged to 19th-Century queens and empresses.

The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security.

articles.title: Actor Simon Pegg reveals ADHD diagnosis: 'It's just who I am'
articles.summary: The Shaun of the Dead and Mission: Impossible films star had previously put symptoms down to "character fault".
articles.body:
Shaun of the Dead and Mission: Impossible films star Simon Pegg has revealed he has been diagnosed with ADHD, which he said "confirmed a lot of stuff that I'd been wrestling with".

Pegg, 56, who also co-created and starred in films Hot Fuzz, The World's End, and TV series Spaced, said "there was a lot of build-up and suspicion, and it just took a while actually to get there."

Speaking on the podcast I'm ADHD! No You're Not on Thursday, he said he pursued a diagnosis as he "just wanted to know".

ADHD symptoms focus on three main areas - inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity plus lack of concentration.

Although many people may feel like they have some similar symptoms, genetics play an important role in ADHD and a full diagnosis is given to those who are negatively affected on a daily basis.

Pegg said he had previously been putting his symptoms down to "just character fault".

The actor and writer also spoke about his mental health, including having clinical depression and struggling to control his drinking, which he said he initially thought had "caused" his diagnosis.

"I felt like it was something that had come on in later life because I wasn't a naughty child.

"I've had bouts of depression in my adult life since 18 and I thought maybe it had come on with that.

"Maybe over the years with therapy and medication - whatever - I've been treating the symptoms and not the cause of why I feel that way."

Pegg said: "I did feel different in a way I might not be able to put my finger on. Maybe everybody feels that way.

"I just assumed ADHD kids were kind of chaotic and difficult and didn't pay attention in school," he added.

"But there were other things that I did do as a kid – fidget or whatever – that made me think, 'Oh no, maybe I've had this longer than I thought'."

Pegg said his wife has been supportive and is "dealing with it as if I'd been diagnosed ages ago", adding: "It's just who I am, and it's just things that I do.

"She makes allowances for forgetfulness and and lack of concentration."

ADHD has rewired the workplace. This is what it means for bosses and workers

Johnny Vegas opens up about recent ADHD diagnosis

Richard Bacon: 'Why I quite like my ADHD'

The star, who has had several speeding convictions, told LBC last year that he felt an ADHD diagnosis would help explain his poor concentration when it comes to driving.

He reversed into a post while on holiday in Greece, which prompted him to look up the symptoms of ADHD.

"I looked up on the phone 'Do people with ADHD get into more car accidents than people who don't have it' and the answer was yes.

"And it's because of a lack of focus and ability to kind of totally focus.

"And that was the final straw that broke my ADHD camel's back. I need to speak to a psychiatrist and find out for sure if I have this thing."

Other celebrities who have been diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood include comedian and actor Johnny Vegas, comic and presenter Sue Perkins, presenters Ant McPartlin and Richard Bacon, comedian Rory Bremner and model Erin O'Connor.

ADHD is described by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) as "a behavioural syndrome characterised by hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention".

The NHS estimates that about 2.5 million people in England have ADHD, including those without a formal diagnosis.

Diagnosis rates of ADHD and autism have soared, and waiting lists for assessments on the NHS in England are at record levels, with lists even closing in some areas due to the huge demand.

Research from University College London suggests nearly a 20-fold increase in the number of UK adults diagnosed with ADHD between 2000 and 2018.

Despite these rises in diagnosis and referrals, some studies suggest ADHD is actually underdiagnosed.

In June, the Lancet Regional Health Europe journal published research suggesting that while around 1.2% of adults in England had an ADHD diagnosis, international prevalence data estimates it affects 3-5% of people. The authors of the study said this indicates it could still be under-diagnosed, particularly in older age groups.

articles.title: From fishing nets to grey-zone tactics: Chinese militia boat enter Taiwan’s sensitive east coast - report
articles.summary: A Chinese fishing boat believed to be part of Beijing’s maritime militia has been spotted operating alongside a coast guard cutter and a research vessel
articles.body: A Chinese fishing boat believed to be part of Beijing’s maritime militia has been spotted operating alongside a coast guard cutter and a research vessel off Taiwan’s Pacific coast, in what appears to be the first known sighting of such a vessel in the strategically sensitive waters.The vessel, identified as the Minfudingyu 07902, was detected more than 30 nautical miles off Taiwan’s eastern Hualien county in August, according to a surveillance report by Taiwan-based Apex Aviation reviewed by Reuters. The report used radar screenshots, infrared imagery and automatic identification system data to track the vessels.The sighting comes as China has stepped up activity along Taiwan’s east coast since June, with regular coast guard patrols in an area Taipei considers crucial for potential wartime supply routes from its allies. Taiwanese officials have said the growing presence of Chinese military, paramilitary and civilian vessels could be part of preparations for a possible maritime blockade.Fishing boat joins Chinese maritime groupThe Minfudingyu 07902 was identified as a fishing vessel that doubles as a Chinese maritime militia boat. According to the Apex report, it was operating alongside Chinese coast guard cutter 2502 and the research vessel Xiang Yang Hong 03 on a day in mid-August.Two senior Taiwanese officials briefed on the incident confirmed that the three vessels had been operating near Taiwan at the time. They said Taiwanese authorities had identified the fishing boat as belonging to the People's Liberation Army's maritime militia fleet.One of the officials said the vessel was operating "in coordination with Chinese coast guard maritime harassment drills"."The purpose of militia boats is to conduct substantive harassment," the official said.The second official said the three vessels were operating "in an area not commonly used by Chinese vessels" and had been "designated for heightened monitoring".The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue.Taiwan's defence ministry told Reuters that China was increasingly using civilian and official vessels together in activities it described as harassment operations.China was "using law enforcement and scientific research as cover for harassment, seeking to expand their scope of operations during a non-conflict scenario to create an illusion of de facto jurisdiction," Taiwan's defence ministry said in a statement.The ministry said such activities undermine international order and challenge Taiwan's maritime rights. It added that Taiwan's military was using reconnaissance capabilities to monitor Chinese activity in coordination with other agencies, including the coast guard.China's Taiwan Affairs Office and defence ministry did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.Why Taiwan’s east coast mattersThe latest sighting is notable because Chinese maritime militia vessels have traditionally been more commonly associated with disputed areas in the South China Sea.Taiwan lies across the Taiwan Strait from mainland China, but its eastern coastline opens into the wider Pacific. Taipei considers these waters strategically important because they could provide access to supply routes from countries supporting Taiwan in the event of a conflict or blockade.Taiwanese officials have increasingly warned that Beijing could seek to rehearse a blockade by combining military, coast guard, maritime militia and civilian vessels.The activity along Taiwan's east coast has intensified since June, when Chinese coast guard vessels began making regular patrols in the area.The presence of a maritime militia boat alongside a coast guard cutter and a research vessel therefore provides another example of the overlapping use of China's maritime assets, according to Taiwanese officials and analysts.China considers Taiwan part of its territory and has not ruled out the use of force to bring the island under its control. Taiwan rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims and maintains its own government and military.What is China’s maritime militia?China's maritime militia is made up largely of fishing vessels whose crews receive training and support to operate in disputed waters.The practice dates back to the 1950s, and the vessels have become a familiar feature around maritime flashpoints in the South China Sea.Analysts say the militia allows Beijing to reinforce its maritime claims while retaining a civilian appearance. Fishing vessels can operate alongside coast guard and other government ships, making it harder to clearly distinguish between civilian activity and state-directed operations.The vessels have previously been observed in disputed waters in the South China Sea, where China has sought to assert its territorial and maritime claims.The August sighting off Taiwan's eastern coast is notable because of the location and the combination of vessels involved.The Taiwanese officials said the Minfudingyu 07902 was already being tracked as part of the PLA's maritime militia fleet.Civilian aircraft tracks Chinese vesselsThe new details emerged from a surveillance operation conducted by Apex Aviation, a Taiwanese company better known for pilot training and charter flights.According to its report, one of the company's reconnaissance aircraft detected a group of Chinese vessels more than 30 nautical miles off Hualien.Apex declined to disclose the precise date of the sighting, citing safety concerns linked to counter-reconnaissance measures against its operations.The company documented the vessels using radar screenshots, infrared imagery and automatic identification system data.The three vessels were spread across an area covering roughly 10 nautical miles, according to Honor Hung, Apex's defence and security director."Chinese warships, coast guard vessels, research ships and some civilian vessels continue to operate in overlapping ways, "creating pressure in the waters surrounding Taiwan"," Hung said.However, he cautioned that a single surveillance operation could not establish what the individual vessels were doing or determine whether the three ships were coordinating their activities.Apex's surveillance aircraft is equipped with a powerful US-made radar capable of detecting objects on the sea surface as small as 900 square centimetres, or about 140 square inches.Taiwan expands surveillance amid China activityThe private patrol also reflects Taiwan's broader effort to involve civilian organisations and companies in capabilities linked to its "whole of society resilience" initiative.The initiative seeks to strengthen Taiwan's ability to respond to potential military and other security contingencies by drawing on resources beyond the armed forces.Apex said its patrols are independently conducted and are not carried out on behalf of the Taiwanese government.Still, the company's surveillance activities provide an additional source of information on Chinese movements around Taiwan at a time when Taipei is closely monitoring the waters surrounding the island.Taiwan's defence ministry said its military was using reconnaissance tools alongside other government agencies to track Chinese activity.Blockade concerns growTaiwanese officials have increasingly focused on the possibility that China could use a combination of military and non-military vessels to restrict access to the island without immediately launching a full-scale invasion.A maritime blockade could potentially target Taiwan's commercial shipping and disrupt the movement of essential supplies while using coast guard and civilian vessels to create pressure around the island.Taiwan's east coast would be particularly important in such a scenario because it faces the Pacific and could serve as an alternative route for supplies and support from Taiwan's partners.The appearance of a Chinese maritime militia vessel in those waters therefore adds to concerns in Taipei about the expanding geographical scope of China's maritime operations.The August patrol does not by itself establish that Beijing was rehearsing a blockade, and Apex said its surveillance could not determine the specific missions of the three vessels.But Taiwanese authorities have placed the vessels under heightened monitoring as China continues to increase maritime activity around the island.You use AI every day. articles.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine ambassador over prisoner-of-war row
articles.summary: It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul.
articles.body:
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.

It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.

Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.

The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.

South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.

And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.

But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga.

In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".

Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia

Thousands of North Koreans fought for Russia. A memorial hints at the death toll

Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".

It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.

President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.

But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.

Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.

The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.

Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.

Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.

After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.

This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.

Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.

South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.

Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

articles.title: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, UKMTO says
articles.summary: Casualties have been reported on the vessel, identified by a maritime intelligence firm as the oil and chemical tanker, Acers.
articles.body:
A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.

The incident - a rare attack deep inside the Gulf - happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal with casualties reported, the UKMTO said.

Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers. On Saturday it was reported as sailing towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.

Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.

At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO).

The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula.

This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group.

Also on Thursday, Vanguard amended an earlier report that had said there was a fire on board another tanker in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.

The company clarified that there were no indications a fire occurred on the vessel, which it had identified as the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler.

articles.body: At least two people were killed after the lower floors of a seven-storey building partially collapsed in Istanbul’s Maltepe district on Thursday, with rescue teams searching for people still believed to be trapped in the rubble, officials said.The building’s three lower floors, including a ground-floor shop, collapsed before dawn in the district on the Asian side of Istanbul. The cause of the collapse was not immediately known and an investigation was underway.Residents on the upper floors were evacuated safely, while rescue teams pulled eight people from the rubble, according to the latest update. articles.title: Seventh man bailed in connection with RAF Fairford incident
articles.summary: A 22 year-old British national was arrested on Tuesday as part of the investigation into the incident near the airbase in Gloucestershire in September.
articles.body:
A 22-year-old British national who was arrested on suspicion of preparing acts of terror in connection with an incident close to RAF Fairford has been released on bail.

The man was arrested in Westminster, London, under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006 on Tuesday, as part of the counter-terror police investigation into the incident near the airbase in Gloucestershire.

In total, seven men - all in their 20s - have been arrested and later bailed in connection with the incident. No one has been charged.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the airbase in the early hours of 27 September.

Five men, aged between 23 and 25, were initially arrested on the day of the incident after vehicles were reported near the base.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing an act of terror.

A sixth man, a 25-year-old dual Iranian-British national, was arrested on 1 October in Westminster. The seventh man, a 22-year-old British national, was arrested in Westminster on Tuesday by counter-terror police.

Both were arrested on suspicion of preparing an act of terror.

RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used by the US Air Force for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

But on Sunday, it emerged the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details.

"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy," he told reporters.

"But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."

Prior to Trump's intervention, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to the US president's previous comments, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.

articles.title: Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
articles.summary: Ukraine accused Russia of targeting the crowded vehicles in the front line city of Kramatorsk to kill as many civilians as possible.
articles.body:
At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.

Authorities said three people were also killed in the village of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community.

Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.

Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Moscow is trying to seize as part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said: "This strike will not go without our response."

In a post on Telegram, he said: "Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this. React harshly - exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have caused."

Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.

Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across the country and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.

According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.

In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, meeting Zelensky in Kyiv on Thursday, said the attack in Pryluky showed Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".

He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict".

After the deadly attack on Kramatorsk, Donetsk regional head Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the eastern front line region to move to safer parts of Ukraine.

Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.

Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.

For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.

Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall. In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.

Kramatorsk City Council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".

"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it said.

Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 22 in block of flats

Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas

Russia is also launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing throughout the day.

Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko said attacks on Thursday had killed three people, with 14 others injured. Two of the eight injured are in a critical condition.

The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport.

Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts.

Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".

Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.

Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have.

Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.

Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.
